title: Participles: middle and passive forms

objectives.can: Parse middle and passive participles of every tense.

explanation.summary: Middle and passive participles are built on three patterns: -ομενος in the present, -σαμενος in the first aorist middle and -μενος in the perfect, all declined like ordinary adjectives, and -θεις in the aorist passive, declined like the active participles. Once you know the four endings, you can parse every middle and passive participle of the New Testament.

sections.heading: Three tenses in -μενος
body: The present middle or passive participle is the present stem plus -ομενος, -ομενη, -ομενον. ἐρχόμενος is nominative singular masculine of ἔρχομαι; λεγόμενος is the same form of λέγω. The perfect middle or passive participle is the perfect stem plus -μενος, -μενη, -μενον, with no connecting vowel. Most verbs show the reduplication at the front, as in δεδεμένος from δέω; where the stem begins with a vowel or with certain consonants, as in εὐλογημένος from εὐλογέω, no extra syllable is visible. The aorist middle participle is the aorist stem plus -σαμενος, -σαμενη, -σαμενον in the first aorist, as in σπασάμενος, and -ομενος in the second aorist, as in γενόμενος.

All of these are adjectives of the pattern ἀγαθός, ἀγαθή, ἀγαθόν: masculine and neuter in -ου, -ῳ, -ον, feminine in -ης, -ῃ, -ην. They are the easiest participles to decline. They are told apart by the stem and by the accent: the perfect has its accent on the next-to-last syllable (-μένος), the first aorist on the α (-σάμενος), the present usually on the connecting vowel (-όμενος).

sections.heading: The aorist passive in -θεις
body: The aorist passive participle has the sign -θ-, as the indicative does, then -εις, -εισα, -εν: πορευθείς, πορευθεῖσα and, in the neuter, ῥηθέν. Like the active participles, the masculine and neuter are third declension, with the stem -θεντ- seen in the genitive: -θέντος. The feminine is -θεῖσα, genitive -θείσης. The accent is always on the ending in the nominative: ἀποκριθείς, πορευθείς. Some verbs have the second aorist passive and drop the θ: the endings are -εις, -εισα, -εν.

The aorist passive participle and the aorist active participle are alike in their third-declension endings, and differ in the sign: -σαντ- in the active, -θεντ- in the passive. Do not take the -ντ- as a sign of the active.

sections.heading: Middle or passive? What the form can and cannot tell you
body: In the present and the perfect, the middle and the passive are one form. λεγόμενος can be 'being said' or 'called' in the passive sense, and ἐρχόμενος is the participle of a verb that is middle in form and active in meaning. Only the verb and the context decide. The analysed text of this course labels each participle with the voice that suits its use: a verb such as ἔρχομαι or πορεύομαι, which has no active in these texts, is labelled middle, and a form like λεγόμενος in Matthew 1:16 is labelled passive. Do not treat the label as a fact about the ending.

In the aorist the forms differ, so the form tells you something. -σαμενος and the second aorist -ομενος are middle forms: γενόμενος, σπασάμενος. -θεις is the passive form. Even so, the passive form does not always have a passive meaning. ἀποκριθείς in Matthew 15:28 has the form of an aorist passive and means 'having answered': Jesus is the one who answers, and he is not answered. The same is true of πορευθείς, 'having gone'. For such verbs the form belongs to the aorist passive and the meaning is active.

sections.heading: A routine for parsing
body: Work from the ending backwards. -θεις or -θεντ-: aorist passive. -σαμενος: first aorist middle. -μενος with a reduplicated stem and the accent on the -μέν- syllable: perfect. -ομενος: present, or second aorist middle; decide by the stem (compare γινόμενος and γενόμενος, the present and the second aorist of the same verb). Then read the case, number and gender from the adjective endings, exactly as for ἀγαθός or, for -θεις, as for the active participles.

misunderstandings: Reading every -μενος participle as passive. Many verbs, such as ἔρχομαι, have middle forms with an active meaning, and a participle like ἐρχόμενος is simply 'coming'.
Reading every -θεις participle as passive in meaning. ἀποκριθείς, 'having answered', is the standard example of a passive form with an active sense.

Treating the perfect participle as present because both end in -μενος. The perfect usually has a reduplicated stem (δεδεμένος) and always lacks the connecting vowel; the present has -ο- before -μενος.
Confusing the active participle -ων with the middle -ομενος. The middle form always has -μεν- in the middle of the ending, and it declines like ἀγαθός, without -ντ-.

deeper.heading: Why the aorist passive is 'passive' in form only
body: The -θη- aorist began as a way of making an intransitive aorist from a verb, and it came to be the usual aorist for the passive. In the New Testament it is also the aorist of many verbs that have no other aorist, whatever their meaning. That is why grammarians describe such forms as passive in form only, and why this lesson asks you to read the form first and the meaning second.
